claim: Radiation damage often limits the resolution and accuracy of macromolecular crystal structures.
source: Radiation damage often limits the resolution and accuracy of macromolecular crystal structures (Garman, 2010; Zeldin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garman, 2010 and Zeldin et al., 2013

claim: Femtosecond X-ray free electron laser (XFEL) pulses enable the possibility of visualizing molecular structures before the onset of radiation damage.
source: Femtosecond X-ray free electron laser (XFEL) pulses enable the possibility of visualizing molecular structures before the onset of radiation damage, and allow the dynamics of chemical processes to be captured (Solem, 1986; Neutze et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Solem, 1986 and Neutze et al., 2000

claim: Most XFEL structures reported to date use a liquid jet to inject small crystals into the beam.
source: Most of the structures reported from XFELs to date use a liquid jet to inject small crystals into the beam (DePonte et al., 2008; Sierra et al., 2012; Weierstall et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to DePonte et al., 2008; Sierra et al., 2012; Weierstall et al., 2014

claim: Diffraction data have been measured from crystals placed in the beam with a standard goniometer setup.
source: but diffraction data have also been measured from crystals placed in the beam with a standard goniometer setup (Cohen et al., 2014; Hirata et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2014 and Hirata et al., 2014

claim: The crystal is effectively stationary during the 10–50 fs exposure in XFEL experiments.
source: Because the crystal is effectively stationary during the 10–50 fs exposure, 'still' diffraction patterns are obtained
evidence: Based on the known properties of XFEL exposure times

claim: An XFEL data set comprises 'still' diffraction patterns generally containing only partially recorded reflections.
source: An XFEL data set comprises 'still' diffraction patterns generally containing only partially recorded reflections, typically from randomly oriented crystals.
evidence: Based on the nature of XFEL data collection described in the manuscript

claim: Most XFEL diffraction data processing approaches have approximated the full intensity by the Monte Carlo method.
source: Most XFEL diffraction data processing approaches reported to date have approximated the full intensity by the so-called "Monte Carlo" method, in which thousands of partial intensity observations of a given reflection are summed and normalized by the number of observations
evidence: Describes the state of the field in XFEL data processing

claim: The Monte Carlo method requires a very large number of crystals to ensure convergence of the averaged partial reflection intensities to the full intensity value.
source: this method requires a very large number of crystals to ensure convergence of the averaged partial reflection intensities to the full intensity value (Kirian et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirian et al., 2010

claim: Shot-to-shot differences in pulse intensity and energy spectrum arise from the self-amplified stimulated emission (SASE) process.
source: Moreover, shot-to-shot differences in pulse intensity and energy spectrum that arise from the self-amplified stimulated emission (SASE) process (Kondratenko and Saldin, 1979; Bonifacio et al., 1984)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kondratenko and Saldin, 1979 and Bonifacio et al., 1984

claim: Post-refinement methods were developed in the 1970s by the Harrison and Rossmann groups.
source: In the 1970's, the Harrison and Rossmann groups developed 'post-refinement' methods (Rossmann et al., 1979; Winkler et al., 1979)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossmann et al., 1979 and Winkler et al., 1979

claim: Post-refinement made it possible to obtain high-quality diffraction data sets collected from many virus crystals.
source: Applied to virus crystals, for which only a few images can typically be collected before radiation damage becomes significant, post-refinement made it possible to obtain high-quality diffraction data sets collected from many crystals (Rossmann et al., 1979; Winkler et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossmann et al., 1979 and Winkler et al., 1979

claim: Other schemes for implementing post-refinement of XFEL diffraction data have been described previously but only applied to simulated XFEL data.
source: Other schemes for implementing post-refinement of XFEL diffraction data have been described previously, but thus far they have been only applied to simulated XFEL data (White, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to White, 2014

claim: Post-refinement has been applied to pseudo-still images collected using monochromatic synchrotron radiation.
source: and to pseudo-still images collected using monochromatic synchrotron radiation (Kabsch, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kabsch, 2014

claim: The authors developed a new post-refinement procedure specifically designed for diffraction data from still images collected from crystals in random orientations.
source: We have developed a new post-refinement procedure specifically designed for diffraction data from still images collected from crystals in random orientations.
evidence: Direct statement of the authors' work

claim: The authors implemented their method in a new computer program called prime (post-refinement and merging).
source: We implemented our method in a new computer program, prime (post-refinement and merging), that post-refines the parameters needed for calculating the partiality of reflections recorded on each still image.
evidence: Direct statement of the authors' implementation

claim: Post-refinement greatly improves the quality of the diffraction data from XFEL diffraction experiments with crystals of three different proteins.
source: We describe here our method and demonstrate that post-refinement greatly improves the quality of the diffraction data from XFEL diffraction experiments with crystals of three different proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The post-refinement procedure allows complete data sets to be extracted from a much smaller number of diffraction images than necessary when using the Monte Carlo method.
source: We show that our post-refinement procedure allows complete data sets to be extracted from a much smaller number of diffraction images than that necessary when using the Monte Carlo method.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing different numbers of images

claim: The partiality model assumes that the measurement is an areal (infinitely thin) sample of the volume.
source: To calculate partiality, we assume that the measurement is an areal (i.e., infinitely thin) sample of the volume (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement of the model assumption with reference to Figure 1B

claim: The maximum partial intensity that can be recorded for a given reflection occurs when its center lies exactly on the Ewald sphere.
source: The maximum partial intensity that can be recorded for a given reflection will occur when its center lies exactly on the Ewald sphere.
evidence: Based on the geometric relationship between reciprocal lattice points and the Ewald sphere

claim: The Ewald offset correction is defined as 1 for any reflection centered on the Ewald sphere.
source: The Eocarea of any reflection centered on the Ewald sphere is defined as 1; this position corresponds to the maximum partial intensity that could be measured for the reflection.
evidence: Direct definition of the Ewald offset correction function

claim: The SASE spectrum emitted by the XFEL is broad and varies from shot-to-shot.
source: The SASE spectrum emitted by the XFEL is broad and varies from shot-to-shot (Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2012

claim: Myoglobin diffraction data were collected from frozen crystals mounted on a standard goniometer setup.
source: Diffraction data for both myoglobin and hydrogenase were collected from frozen crystals mounted on a standard goniometer setup (Cohen et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2014

claim: Thermolysin data were collected using an electrospun liquid jet to inject nanocystals into a vacuum chamber.
source: whereas the thermolysin data were collected using an electrospun liquid jet to inject nanocystals into a vacuum chamber (Sierra et al., 2012; Bogan, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sierra et al., 2012 and Bogan, 2013

claim: The partiality model target function Tpr markedly decreased in the first microcycle and fully converged in the last microcycle for myoglobin.
source: The partiality model target function Tpr (Equation 1) markedly decreased in the first microcycle and fully converged in the last microcycle.
evidence: Observation from the convergence analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: The spot position residual Txy decreased both during post-refinement of the crystal orientation and the unit-cell parameters.
source: The spot position residual Txy (Equation 2), also decreased both during post-refinement of the crystal orientation and the unit-cell parameters.
evidence: Observation from the convergence analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: For myoglobin using all 757 images, the CC1/2 value improved after post-refinement, especially for reflections in the low-resolution shells.
source: For the myoglobin diffraction data set using all 757 images (Table 2, Figure 6A,B), the CC1/2 value improved after post-refinement, especially for those reflections in the low-resolution shells (Figure 5C; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Table 2

claim: The real-space correlation coefficient of the heme group to the difference maps calculated from the post-refined diffraction data sets is higher than that calculated from the corresponding averaged merged diffraction data sets.
source: The real-space correlation coefficient of the heme group to the difference maps calculated from the post-refined diffraction data sets is higher than that calculated from the corresponding averaged merged diffraction data sets using the same set of diffraction images (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The post-refined diffraction data set produced the best Rfree and Rwork values for myoglobin.
source: The post-refined diffraction data set produced the best Rfree and Rwork values, followed by the mean-scaled partiality corrected, with the averaged merged diffraction data sets yielding the poorest refinement statistics.
evidence: Supported by refinement statistics in Table 2

claim: Post-refinement is superior to methods that only consider each diffraction image individually.
source: Thus, post-refinement against the iteratively improved reference set is superior to methods that only consider each diffraction image individually, even when the reflections are scaled and corrected for partiality.
evidence: Inference from comparison of different data processing methods

claim: 100 diffraction images are sufficient for myoglobin structure refinement.
source: Given the significant improvements obtained by post-refining all available images, we tested whether accurate diffraction data and refined atomic models could be obtained using fewer diffraction images by post-refining the randomly selected subset of 100 myoglobin diffraction images.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using 100 images

claim: The real-space correlation coefficient of the heme group with the difference map obtained with the post-refined 100 diffraction images is better than that calculated from the averaged merged diffraction data set using all 757 diffraction images.
source: Moreover, the real-space correlation coefficient of the heme group with the difference map obtained with the post-refined 100 diffraction images is better than that calculated from the averaged merged diffraction data set using all the 757 diffraction images (Figure 6A), despite the higher completeness and CC1/2 value of the latter data set (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 5C

claim: Post-refinement both improves diffraction data quality for a given set of images and reduces the number of diffraction images required for structure determination.
source: Thus, post-refinement both improves diffraction data quality for a given set of images and reduces the number of diffraction images required for structure determination and refinement from serial diffraction data.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental comparisons

claim: The omit maps and real-space correlation coefficients for the heme group were of comparable quality between post-refined XFEL data and synchrotron data.
source: The omit maps and real-space correlation coefficients for the heme group were of comparable quality (Figure 7).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 7

claim: XFEL diffraction data for hydrogenase were measured from eight crystals using a goniometer-mounted fixed-target grid.
source: XFEL diffraction data for Clostridium pasteurianum hydrogenase were measured from eight crystals by the Peters (University of Montana) and SSRL-SMB groups using a goniometer-mounted fixed-target grid (Cohen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2014

claim: The hydrogenase experiment generated 177 diffraction images that could be merged to a completeness of 91%.
source: This experiment generated 177 diffraction images that could be merged to a completeness of 91%, with more than half of the diffraction images containing reflections to 1.6 Å
evidence: Data from the hydrogenase experiment

claim: The CC1/2 value improved significantly with post-refinement for hydrogenase.
source: The CC1/2 value improved significantly with post-refinement (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 3

claim: The omit map densities for the post-refined hydrogenase diffraction data sets clearly show the entire Fe-S cluster whereas the densities using the averaged merged data sets are much poorer.
source: The omit map densities for the post-refined diffraction data sets using the complete set of 177 diffraction images and the randomly selected subset of 100 diffraction images (83% complete) clearly show the entire Fe-S cluster whereas the densities using the averaged merged data sets are much poorer (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8A

claim: The R and Rfree values for both post-refined hydrogenase data sets were significantly better than the averaged merged case.
source: Upon atomic model refinement with the Fe-S clusters and water molecules included, the R and Rfree values for both post-refined data sets were significantly better than the averaged merged case (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8B

claim: The thermolysin diffraction data were collected at a photon energy just above the absorption edge of zinc.
source: The thermolysin diffraction data were collected at a photon energy just above the absorption edge of zinc
evidence: Description of experimental conditions

claim: Post-refinement improved the peak heights of both the zinc and calcium ions in thermolysin.
source: Post-refinement improved the peak heights of both the zinc and calcium ions (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 4

claim: Two anomalous difference peaks near the active site above 3 σ were observed using the post-refined thermolysin data sets.
source: We observed two anomalous difference peaks near the active site above 3 σ using the post-refined data sets.
evidence: Observation from anomalous difference Fourier maps

claim: The second, smaller anomalous peak in thermolysin is not visible in the anomalous difference map using the 'averaged-merged' data set with 2000 images.
source: In contrast, the second, smaller peak is not visible in the anomalous difference map using the 'averaged-merged' data set with 2000 images
evidence: Comparison of anomalous difference maps

claim: The second anomalous peak had not been clearly visible in the previous data analysis of the thermolysin XFEL data set (PDB ID: 4OW3).
source: and it had not been clearly visible in the previous data analysis of the thermolysin XFEL data set (PDB ID: 4OW3; Hattne et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison with previously published structure, supported by citation to Hattne et al., 2014

claim: A previous thermolysin structure (PDB ID: 1LND) reported two zinc sites in the active site.
source: A previous thermolysin structure (PDB ID: 1LND; Holland et al., 1995) reported two zinc sites in the active site that correspond to the two anomalous-difference peaks observed with our post-refined data set.
evidence: Supported by citation to Holland et al., 1995

claim: A Leu–Lys dipeptide was observed in the electron density near the active site of thermolysin.
source: When the molecular replacement model of thermolysin was refined against the post-refined data, we observed a well-connected electron density feature in the mFo-DFc map near the active site.
evidence: Observation from difference electron density maps

claim: In the deposited thermolysin model (PDB ID: 4OW3), weak density features near the active site were interpreted as water molecules.
source: In contrast, in the deposited model refined against the original XFEL data (Hattne et al., 2014; PDB ID: 4OW3), weak density features in this region were interpreted as water molecules.
evidence: Comparison with previously published structure, supported by citation to Hattne et al., 2014

claim: The dipeptide had a higher real-space correlation coefficient with the maps calculated from the post-refined diffraction data than those calculated from the averaged merged diffraction data.
source: The dipeptide had a higher real-space correlation coefficient (CC) with the maps calculated from the post-refined diffraction data than those calculated from the averaged merged diffraction data.
evidence: Comparison of real-space correlation coefficients

claim: The electron density for both post-refined thermolysin diffraction data sets is better connected than that of the averaged merged diffraction data set.
source: The electron density for both post-refined diffraction data sets is also better connected than that of the averaged merged diffraction data set (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 10A

claim: The Rwork and Rfree values of the refined complete thermolysin model using the post-refined diffraction data are lower than those using the averaged merged data throughout the entire resolution range.
source: The Rwork and Rfree values of the refined complete model using the post-refined diffraction data are lower than those using the averaged merged data throughout the entire resolution range (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 10B

claim: When completeness is high, adding more images to increase the multiplicity of observations has only a modest impact on the quality of the final refined structures using the post-refined diffraction data.
source: When completeness is high, adding more images to increase the multiplicity of observations has only a modest impact on the quality of the final refined structures using the post-refined diffraction data.
evidence: Observation from analysis of subsets with varying numbers of images

claim: For thermolysin subsets ranging from 2000 to 12,000 diffraction images (all 100% complete at 2.6 Å), the peak height in the omit map, CC1/2 values, and R values did not improve significantly when more than 8000 images were used.
source: For example, when subsets ranging from 2000 to 12,000 thermolysin diffraction images (all subsets 100% complete at 2.6 Å) were post-refined the peak height in the omit map for the larger of the two anomalous sites (Figure 11C), the CC1/2 values, and the R values of the refined structures did not improve significantly when more than 8000 images were used.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 11

claim: Processing of XFEL diffraction data requires new methods and implementations.
source: In contrast, processing of XFEL diffraction data, which are collected from crystals in random orientations as 'still' diffraction images, requires new methods and implementations such as those described here.
evidence: Statement about the need for new methods in XFEL crystallography

claim: Improved data collection and processing methods are important for making XFELs useful for challenging investigations in structural biology.
source: Improved data collection and processing methods, particularly those that can significantly reduce the amount of sample needed to assemble a complete and accurate diffraction data set, are important for making XFELs useful for certain challenging investigations in structural biology.
evidence: Statement about the importance of method development

claim: The authors' implementation of post-refinement differs from that of Kabsch (2014).
source: Kabsch uses a partiality model in which an Ewald offset correction is defined as a Gaussian function of angular distance from the Ewald sphere.
evidence: Comparison with Kabsch's method

claim: The authors' implementation of post-refinement differs from that of White (2014).
source: White used the intersecting volume between the reflection and the limiting-energy Ewald spheres defined by the energy spectrum for the partiality calculation, and calculates the initial reference data set by averaging all observations without scaling.
evidence: Comparison with White's method

claim: Neither Kabsch (2014) nor White (2014) describe an application to experimental XFEL diffraction data.
source: Neither report describes an application to experimental XFEL diffraction data, so we cannot compare these methods to the results presented here.
evidence: Statement about the lack of experimental validation in previous reports

claim: The authors' implementation of post-refinement substantially improves the quality of the diffraction data from three different XFEL experiments.
source: We have demonstrated here that our implementation of post-refinement substantially improves the quality of the diffraction data from three different XFEL experiments.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: The resulting structures can be refined to significantly lower Rfree and R values with electron density maps that reveal novel features more clearly than those using non-post-refined XFEL data sets.
source: Moreover, the resulting structures can be refined to significantly lower Rfree and R values, with electron density maps that reveal novel features more clearly, than those using non-post-refined XFEL data sets.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: A key feature of the authors' method is that the parameters that define the diffracted spot are iteratively refined against the reference set.
source: A key feature of our method is that the parameters that define the diffracted spot are iteratively refined against the reference set.
evidence: Description of the method

claim: This development will make XFEL crystallography accessible to many challenging problems in biology for which sample quantity is a major limiting factor.
source: Thus, this development will make XFEL crystallography accessible to many challenging problems in biology for which sample quantity is a major limiting factor.
evidence: Conclusion about the impact of the method

claim: The comparison of myoglobin omit maps suggests that synchrotron data are perhaps somewhat better than XFEL data.
source: The comparison of myoglobin omit maps (Figure 7) suggests that the SR data are perhaps somewhat better
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 7

claim: Rotation data would likely be better than still data due to the ability to directly measure full reflections without modeling partiality.
source: We suspect that rotation data would be better due to the ability to directly measure full reflections (at least by summation of partials) without modeling partiality, which is still a relatively crude process
evidence: Speculation about the relative merits of rotation vs still data

claim: The formulation of post-refinement employs the simplifying assumption that reflections are spherical volumes.
source: Our formulation of post-refinement employs the simplifying assumption that reflections are spherical volumes.
evidence: Description of the model assumption

claim: Crystal mosaicity has three components, each with a distinct effect on the reciprocal lattice point.
source: More sophisticated models consider crystal mosaicity to have three components, each with a distinct effect on the reciprocal lattice point (Juers et al., 2007; Nave, 1998, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Juers et al., 2007 and Nave, 1998, 2014

claim: Domain size produces reciprocal lattice points of constant, finite size.
source: First, the domain size (the average size of the coherently scattering mosaic blocks) produces reciprocal lattice points of constant, finite size: small domains produce large-sized spots, while large domains produce small spots, as there is an inverse (Fourier) relation between spot size and domain size.
evidence: Description of the relationship between domain size and spot size based on Fourier theory

claim: Unit-cell variation among domains produces reflections that are spheres whose radii increase with distance from the origin.
source: Second, unit-cell variation among domains produces reflections that are spheres whose radii increase with distance from the origin.
evidence: Description of the effect of unit-cell variation

claim: In cctbx.xfel, mosaicity and effective domain size are taken into account when predicting which reflections are in diffracting position prior to integration.
source: In cctbx.xfel, mosaicity (modeled as isotropic parameter) and effective domain size are taken into account when predicting which reflections are in diffracting position prior to integration (Sauter et al., 2014; Sauter, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sauter et al., 2014 and Sauter, 2015

claim: Orientational spread among mosaic domains produces spots shaped like spherical caps.
source: Third, orientational spread among mosaic domains produces spots shaped like spherical caps.
evidence: Description of the effect of orientational spread

claim: Anisotropy in crystal mosaicity is not considered in the current model.
source: In addition, anisotropy in crystal mosaicity is not considered; this would require refining separate parameters along each lattice direction.
evidence: Statement about limitations of the current model

claim: The rugged energy spectrum that results from the SASE process of the XFEL is not yet considered in the current model.
source: Finally, the rugged energy spectrum that results from the SASE process of the XFEL is not yet considered in our current model.
evidence: Statement about limitations of the current model

claim: The XFEL beam at LCLS is strongly polarized in the horizontal plane.
source: The primary XFEL beam at LCLS is strongly polarized in the horizontal plane
evidence: Description of LCLS beam properties

claim: For a stationary crystal and a monochromatic beam, a Lorentz factor correction is not applicable.
source: For a stationary crystal and a monochromatic beam, a Lorentz factor correction is not applicable
evidence: Based on crystallographic theory for still diffraction

claim: The spectral dispersion of the SASE beam (δE/E ∼ 3 × 10−3) is accounted for by the γe term.
source: the spectral dispersion of the SASE beam (δE/E ∼ 3 × 10−3 for the data sets studied here) is accounted for by the γe term
evidence: Description of how spectral dispersion is modeled

claim: The computer program prime is implemented as a part of the cctbx computational crystallography toolbox.
source: The computer program, prime, is implemented as a part of the cctbx computational crystallography toolbox (Grosse-Kunstleve et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grosse-Kunstleve et al., 2002

claim: Molecular replacement was carried out with Phaser using default settings, with r.m.s.d. set to 0.8.
source: Molecular replacement was carried out with Phaser (McCoy et al., 2007) using default settings, with r.m.s.d. set to 0.8.
evidence: Description of the molecular replacement protocol, supported by citation to McCoy et al., 2007

claim: The standard deviation of the Ewald offset distribution for myoglobin after post-refinement is 0.0016 1/Å or approximately 0.12°.
source: The standard deviation is 0.0016 1/Å or approximately 0.12° (when calculated with the mean of the energy distribution).
evidence: Data from Figure 12 caption
